reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Green's Operative Hand Surgery
clinicalPearls: A benign tumour arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body, a thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunt
The classic triad is paroxysmal pain, marked cold sensitivity, and exquisite pinpoint tenderness, most often at a subungual site of the fingertip
A small bluish or reddish subungual discolouration with associated nail ridging is a helpful clinical sign
Love's pin test localises the point of maximal tenderness and Hildreth's sign is relief of pain when a tourniquet is inflated
MRI shows a small lesion with high signal on T2 and avid enhancement, useful for occult or recurrent tumours
Multiple lesions (glomangiomas) tend to be less painful, may be familial, and are associated with germline glomulin mutations
Histology shows sheets of uniform glomus cells around vascular channels, positive for smooth muscle actin and negative for S100
Complete surgical excision relieves the pain and is curative, with recurrence usually indicating incomplete removal
reference.pathophysiology: The glomus body is a specialised arteriovenous anastomosis in the dermis, particularly concentrated in the digits, that shunts blood to regulate temperature; it is composed of afferent and efferent vessels surrounded by rounded glomus cells, which are modified vascular smooth muscle cells. A glomus tumour is a benign neoplastic proliferation of these glomus cells arranged around vascular spaces. The dense innervation and contractile nature of the constituent cells are thought to underlie the characteristic paroxysmal pain and temperature sensitivity, provoked by contraction in response to cold or pressure. Solitary tumours are typically well circumscribed and predominantly cellular, whereas the multiple glomangioma variant is more vascular and is linked to loss-of-function variants in the glomulin gene. Malignant glomus tumours are exceptionally rare and are recognised by deep location, large size, atypical mitoses, and marked nuclear atypia.
additionalDifferentials: Other painful subcutaneous tumours such as angioleiomyoma, angiolipoma, and neuroma
Foreign body granuloma or chronic paronychia
Neuroma or causalgia of the digit
additionalInvestigations: Focused clinical tests including Love's pin test and Hildreth's sign
MRI to localise small or recurrent subungual lesions
High-resolution ultrasound as an accessible alternative for localisation
Plain radiography to detect any bony scalloping of the distal phalanx
Histology and immunohistochemistry for smooth muscle actin with absent S100
Genetic assessment for glomulin variants when lesions are multiple or familial
redFlags: A deep-seated or large glomus tumour, or one with atypical or necrotic features suggesting malignancy
Rapid growth or the development of numerous new lesions
Persistent or recurrent pain after excision indicating residual tumour
Pigmented subungual lesion where melanoma must be excluded
reference.prognosis: Solitary glomus tumours are benign and complete excision reliably abolishes the pain; recurrence almost always reflects incomplete resection rather than aggressive biology. Malignant glomus tumours are extremely rare but can metastasise and carry a guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Prolonged diagnostic delay, with fingertip pain misattributed to trauma or a psychological cause
Incomplete excision leaving residual tumour and persistent symptoms
Overlooking a subungual melanoma masquerading as a pigmented digital lesion
Confusing the soft tissue glomus tumour with paraganglioma of the head and neck, an unrelated entity sometimes loosely called a glomus tumour
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment and reliably abolishes the pain for solitary lesions
Preoperative MRI or high-resolution ultrasound to localise small, occult or recurrent lesions before surgery
Meticulous complete resection, since recurrence almost always reflects residual tumour rather than aggressive biology
Interim analgesia with avoidance of cold and pressure that provoke the paroxysmal pain
Histological confirmation with immunohistochemistry, and wider excision with oncological follow-up for the rare malignant variant
For multiple glomangiomas consider sclerotherapy or laser as alternatives, and offer genetic assessment and counselling for glomulin variants given familial inheritance
